en: The śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.

Having thus explained [the preceding], what are their characteristics? The commentary states: Among the separate explanations of the six categories of mental factors (*caitasika*), the discussion of the three gates has been concluded.
This is now the fourth [section]. First, it concludes the previous section and poses the question.
The subsequent [sections] may be understood according to the text.
Next, the verses and so forth are cited.
Treatise.
The verse says: "Up to delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view.
The commentary states:
In the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* and other texts, delusion (*moha*) is taught as following pride (*māna*),
because it manifests in both the sharp and dull faculties and pervades all levels, from the highest to the lowest.
This clarifies that because they are unwholesome roots, they are placed above pride (*māna*).
The prose section below provides the explanation.
Within this explanation, there are three parts.
First, the explanation of how the afflictions receive their names,
which interprets the first two characters of the verse.
Second, the determination of their essential nature and function, which explains the remainder of the verse beginning with the word "called" (謂).
The third section extensively analyzes and clarifies these six meanings.
The treatise states: "One attains the name 'affliction' (kleśa)."
The commentary states:
This explains the general name;
that is to say, because these six—greed and the others—are the roots of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Although they may also be termed secondary afflictions (upakleśa), they are subsumed under the primary afflictions (mūlakleśa) and are not merely of the nature of outflows (niṣyanda);
thus, while they receive the name "affliction," they are not called "secondary afflictions."
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter seven, states:
"All afflictions (*kleśa*) are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
however, there are secondary afflictions that are not afflictions."
By this it is shown that what is called "root" is also designated as "secondary," because it arises in accordance with others.
Anger and the others are merely called secondary afflictions (upakleśa) and not root afflictions (kleśa),
because they are not fundamental.
Treatise.
"What is greed, and how does it have the function of producing suffering?
The commentary states:
This is the second section from here on.
The six [factors] are explained as six;
within these, there are two for each.
First, their essential nature and function are set forth.
Subsequently, when it is difficult to distinguish which [of two things] is being referred to—
such as when both the essence (*svabhāva*) and the activity (*karman*) are questioned regarding existence (*bhava*), the means of existence (*bhavopakarana*),
and so forth— one answers both in each case.
However, there are points of difficulty which shall be resolved through further discussion. Regarding "existence" (*bhava*):
this refers to future existence, which is exclusively the fruit of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) as maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding "the equipment for existence" (*bhavopakarana*):
That is, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
along with afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma,
as well as the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) and so forth.
Because they possess the "possessions of existence" (*bhavopakarana*), or because they are untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).

As stated in the latter part of the treatise: those that arise together with views and so forth, taking the untainted as their object, and those that give rise to craving by taking [existence] as their object, are all called "possessions of existence."
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school maintain that [this] takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object;
they hold that greed is actually the desire for wholesome dharmas.
Now, the Mahāyāna explains:
Attachment to the Buddha and craving for cessation are both subsumed under defilement because they arise in association with views and take uncontaminated phenomena as their object. Furthermore,
uncontaminated phenomena can nourish and increase existence, and are thus also called "requisites for existence."
Regarding the fact that [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*], in its fifty-eighth verse and others, does not state that this greed takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object,
the subsequent text will naturally resolve this. Treatise:
This means that the aggregates of grasping arise by the power of craving.
The commentary states:
"If one initiates karma..."
If it moistens birth,
it causes the aggregates of grasping to arise;
it does not mean that it only moistens the afflictions.
In the two upper realms,
because of craving for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth,
those afflictions increase by means of this, and the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) are likewise produced.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chapter 8, 55, and 58), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Pañcaskandhaka*, and the *Abhidharma* all explain the characteristics of craving (*rāga*) in detail.
However, Chapter 8 of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is identical to this [present work].
Treatise:
What is hatred? It has as its function reaching its objective basis.
Commentary: [As follows:]
Regarding those who possess the instruments of suffering:
"suffering" refers to the three types of suffering,
all of which arise from hatred.
It increases only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*),
because hatred (*dveṣa*) also arises based upon it when there is separation from pleasant feelings (*sukhavedanā*).
As for the instruments of suffering:
All contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena that are capable of producing suffering are instruments of suffering.
Based on this, hatred arises. Question: Conditioned phenomena that accord with suffering may be called instruments of suffering;
however, untainted phenomena do not accord with suffering.

Question: How is it called an "instrument of suffering" (*duḥkha-sādhana*)? Answer: It is that which accords with the instruments of suffering. That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is not [such an instrument]. Because it conditions the arising of suffering, [it is so called].
The untainted is likewise so;
therefore, false views and the like that slander the untainted as non-existent bring about the suffering of the miserable realms.
Furthermore, fifty-eight [types of] delusion take the truths of cessation and the path as their objects;
because hatred also takes cessation and the path as its objects of intense aversion and envy,
it is also said that the untainted (anāsrava) serves as the instrument of suffering.
The Abhidharma-samuccaya and other treatises merely state that they are "instruments of suffering," without specifying what they are; consequently,
those who are confused claim they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
This is not so; it is the same in the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The fifty-eighth [fascicle] states:
"There are four."
That is to say, when others perceive sentient beings as being harmful toward those they love or beneficial toward those they dislike,
[the affliction] arises merely by taking that perception as its object.
However, that [previous statement] was still restricted to speech regarding grave matters;
the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* also states that it takes only sentient beings as its object, speaking from the perspective of what constitutes a grave course of action (*karmapatha*).
It is not that there is no aversion toward other [objects]. The treatise states:
this is because aversion necessarily causes one to fall into the nature of unwholesomeness.
The commentary states:
Hatred necessarily gives rise to karma that is subsumed under the nature of unwholesomeness,
because that which incites evil karma is necessarily unwholesome.
The mental consciousness acts as the primary driver (pravṛtti), while the five sensory consciousnesses act as the secondary drivers (anuvartaka).
This is as stated in the first [chapter] of the *Mahāśāstra*. "Not abiding" means...
It is not tranquil. According to the Abhidharma,
because one harbors hatred and anger and dwells much in suffering,
this aversion serves as the basis for misconduct and lack of tranquility.
Treatise:
What is delusion (*moha*), and what is its function? It serves as the basis for [the other afflictions].
Commentary: [As follows:]
Regarding "delusion with respect to principles and phenomena":
this means that independent ignorance (mūla-avidyā) is deluded regarding principles,
while associated ignorance and the others are likewise deluded regarding phenomena.
Treatise:
This refers to [the process] from ignorance up to the phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Commentary states:
This explains the preceding karma:
that is to say, through ignorance one wavers regarding the truths and so forth,
and through wrong view one denies their existence.
Subsequently, residual greed and other afflictions arise in succession,
whereby various unwholesome karmas are committed,
which in turn invite the various defilements of future births.
This refers to the sequence of the arising of ignorance within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
However, this is not necessarily the case for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because doubt and wrong resolve do not necessarily arise therein;
rather, it is through ignorance that craving and the other afflictions arise.
The karma of humans and devas that invites rebirth is defiled;
however, in the Abhidharma,
because ignorance is predominant in those with wrong view.
It is said that doubt arises only after one has first [encountered] wrong concentration;
however, this textual passage regarding the order of arising is correct.
As it says in [the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*], fascicle 58:
There are four kinds of ignorance,
including those that are associated and those that are non-associated;
however, these have already been analyzed in detail in the fifth fascicle concerning the seventh consciousness.
This is not explained in detail here.
However, in various treatises, pride is taught immediately after greed and hatred;
in this context, it is taught immediately after [the other two] simply because it shares the same nature as an unwholesome root, namely ignorance.
In the fifty-eighth and eighth [chapters] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
both have "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) as their primary subject.
Because they are deluded by gain,
they are further subsumed under the seven kinds of ignorance and so forth,
as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra*.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and other texts state:
"What is conceit (*māna*)? Its function is to give rise to suffering."
The commentary states:
It is that which can obstruct non-pride. What is non-pride?
As stated in the *Kuśalamūla-nirdeśa-śāstra*:
"It is said that if there is conceit (*māna*), one will eventually undergo various sufferings."
The commentary states:
Regarding the dharmas of supreme excellence and those who possess such excellence.
Because the mind is not humble, it undergoes manifold sufferings;
this is shown so that one may cultivate weary detachment and no longer transmigrate.
However, in the Abhidharma, it is held that the mind becomes haughty solely because of the notion of a self (*ātman*).
In this context, what is referred to as being associated with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and arising as its outflow (*niṣyanda*) is stated either by way of its remote root cause.
Treatise:
This differentiation of pride arises when it reaches the sphere of one's own virtues.
Commentary: [As stated above].
There are seven and nine kinds;
they do not exceed arising upon the five dharmas,
namely the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.
And myself. We are all born in places of supreme excellence.
What is the meaning of this?
As stated in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*:
among the seven types of pride, the first pride arises from the inferior and middling grades;
that is, one who is inferior imagines themselves to be superior.
Regarding those who are equal, one considers oneself equal;
regarding those of middling or superior quality, one gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
namely, considering oneself superior to those who are equal.
To consider oneself equal to one who is superior is *māna*;
to give rise to pride toward those who are superior is *atimāna*,
which means to consider oneself superior to those who are superior.
Regarding my aggregates, he gives rise to the conceit of "I am," relying on himself with haughty arrogance; thus,
regarding qualities not yet realized, [he is deluded].
They give rise to overweening pride;
although they have attained only a small portion,
they claim to have already attained what they have not yet attained.
One gives rise to the pride of inferiority toward those of superior grade,
thinking that while others are for the most part superior to oneself, one is only slightly inferior.
To claim one possesses virtues when one lacks them is to give rise to false pride;
this false pride consists entirely in asserting that one has what one does not have.
Those with overweening pride consider themselves to have already attained slight excellence,
yet claim it to be manifold and superior;
this is the distinction between the two.
However, four [kinds of knowledge] arise regarding the three categories;
one arises regarding cessation;
and two arise regarding qualities.
The seven types of pride arise with respect to five bases. Regarding the nine types of pride, no textual passage is found within the Mahāyāna [treatises].
The first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*) states:
As the Sūtra states regarding the three types of pride:
"I am superior," "I am equal."
Regarding those of inferior pride (*hīna-māna*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol.
199) and the nineteenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* state that there are nine types of pride (*māna*).
The first three constitute three categories:
superior, equal, and inferior; and another three: non-superior, non-equal, and non-inferior.
Excessive pride (*adhimāna*), pride (*māna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*) correspond respectively to the first three;
inferiority pride, pride, and excessive pride correspond respectively to the middle three;
and pride, excessive pride, and inferiority pride correspond respectively to the last three.
Based on both the *Mūlaśāstra* and the *Prakaraṇapāda*, these two explanations are extensive;
however, the nine [types of pride] arise subsequent to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and originate from three categories of objects.
There is no fault in its being associated with various views. According to the treatise,
there is also no fault in its pervading all [states] up to its arising.
The commentary states:
Within that Hinayāna system, although there exist afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation,
the noble ones do not engage in them.
Because there is no conceit regarding the path of cultivation [in the Hīnayāna],
whereas now, since conceit regarding the self exists even during the cultivation of the Mahāyāna path,
it is therefore manifested by the Noble Ones.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and others state that the seven types of pride are either innate (*sahaja*) or discursive (*vikalpita*).

Therefore, it is known that there is no fault in the cultivation and arising of the nine types of pride. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* explains the fifty-eight [types of pride] with somewhat greater detail by distinguishing their specific characteristics.
[The text asks:
"What is doubt? It is that which prevents the arising of wholesome states."
The commentary states:
Herein, it is explained that doubt is hesitation regarding the principles of the truths.
Among the fifty-eight [types], they are distinguished according to five characteristics.
That is to say: other worlds, activity, cause and effect, the truths, and the jewels.
Herein, the mention of the "truths" (satya) also encompasses all of these;
this should be reflected upon according to reason.
This refers to the doubt that both the principle and the phenomenon are [identical];
however, the doubt that a tree stump is a person is not this kind of doubt.
Alternatively, it refers to the *vipāka*-mind and so forth.
According to one interpretation in the treatise, this doubt persists until it is designated as "doubt."
The commentary states:
Doubt has wisdom as its essence. Why is this so?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states that the discernment of hesitation is termed "doubt" (*vicikitsā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, identifies its essence as "discernment" (*vitarka*);
this "discernment" is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
Decisive judgment is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, discernment and hesitation are distinct,
for decisive cognitive awareness is said to be doubt (*vicikitsā*).
This is proven by the text.
Furthermore, in the *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis), the treatise states:
Because *prajñā* and *mati* do not differ in their ultimate meaning.
The commentary states:
what is called *mati* is a synonym for wisdom (*prajñā*).
It has no separate essence from *prajñā*.
The syllable *vi* is added as an auxiliary to *hui* (wisdom).
*Vi* carries the meaning of "various" or "manifold."
This refers to various types of wisdom (*nānā-prajñā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that "different wisdom" (*anya-prajñā*) means "doubt.
Here, "different" (*anya*) carries the sense of "various" (*nānā*).
Therefore, one should know that the essence of doubt is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is because *mati* and *prajñā* are both synonyms for wisdom,
and the prefix *vi-* serves to distinguish it.
How could there be a separate entity?
This is a divergent teacher within the Mahāyāna,
not a distinct school.
Treatise:
There is an interpretation that this doubt does not constitute wisdom (*prajñā*) itself.
Commentary states:
There is a distinct intrinsic nature;
however, the mention of "hesitation" and "discernment" is due to simultaneous doubt.
Alternatively, because doubt at another time prevents wisdom from reaching a decision,
it is not [itself] wisdom. Thus says the treatise.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that [the afflictions] exist as distinct entities.
The commentary says:
among the six afflictions described in the fifty-fifth [chapter],...
This [perception] is seen as conventionally existent.
Furthermore, he himself explains that it is a constituent of wisdom;
thus, the other five are substantially existent.
Since that [author] himself also explains that there is a distinct nature [of doubt],
we know that the essence of doubt is not identical to wisdom (*prajñā*).
If it were identical to wisdom, [it would be as follows].
It should be stated that [doubt] exists conventionally, just like the five views.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The essence of doubt is not identical to wisdom."
Because among the six afflictions, it is not said that they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*), just like the four [afflictions] beginning with greed (*rāga*). According to the treatise,
*prajñā* (wisdom) derived from *vi-ava-mṛd* should be understood as consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the etymological explanation of the term,
because you hold that *mati* is wisdom (*prajñā*) and [the prefix] *vi-* assists it, you claim that the essence of wisdom is doubt.
Likewise, if "nam" (to bend) signifies wisdom (*jñāna*),
then because it is assisted by "vi," wisdom is said to be consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"Vi" carries the meaning of "various" (*nānārtha*).
Because it assists cognition (*jñāna*), it is designated by the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);
its essence is not identical to cognition.
Why then assist *mati* [thinking], while suspecting that its essence is identical to wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Furthermore, *vijiti* has the meaning of "curing," while *vivicitsā* has the meaning of "doubt.
How could it be assisted by the word *vi*?
The essence of doubt is itself its remedy. According to the treatise,
the realm [of doubt] consists of non-wisdom as its essence, reaching that state through the assistance of other factors.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, *matr* and so forth are verbal roots (*dhātu*).
A root has the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*).
Because the syllable *vi* is the condition (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the power of the assisting element (*dhātu*) undergoes transformation. What is this condition?
Once the assisting element has been applied, the essence remains as it was before.
Therefore, this doubt is not identical to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This master’s explanation of doubt is the same as that found in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharmasamuccaya*).
Treatise:
What is meant by "evil views culminate in having suffering as their karmic result"?
Commentary: [As follows:]
The text contains two parts:
first, the general;
second, the specific.
If it is wholesome, its characteristics are the opposite of those of the unwholesome.
The unwholesome is exclusively non-virtuous;
if it involves censure or reproach, it is termed "evil."
The unwholesome (*akuśala*) includes that which is obscured (*nivṛta*).
Now, these five views are called "unwholesome" because they are designated as such by way of their derogatory nature.
Those who engage in inverted speculation regarding the principles of the truths are simply deluded about those principles;
although there is a distinction between direct and indirect objects of cognition, [the object remains the same].
Because they are deluded regarding the meaning of the principles and so forth. The treatise states:
this is because those with evil views undergo much suffering.
The commentary states:
This explains the preceding karma;
that is to say, within the desire realm.
This excludes only those [afflictions] that are co-emergent,
for they give rise to karma that brings about the locus of suffering;
these are afflictions of conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, those with wrong views mostly give rise to suffering;
this is the general explanation.
However, to explain it specifically:
Treatise:
There are five distinctions in the characteristics of this mode of viewing.
Commentary states:
This is the general heading. The treatise states:
"First, the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which functions as the basis [for other afflictions]."
The commentary states:
Below follows a detailed explanation in four parts,
as the two types of grasping are combined.
In Sanskrit, it is called *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
The Sautrāntika masters state that *sat* has the meaning of "false."
*Kāya* means body (*śarīra*).
*Darśana* means seeing (*darśana*).
Body has the sense of an accumulation (*caya*).
This is a provisional aggregation;
one should say that a view arises conditioned by the collection [of aggregates],
and this is called the false view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
The Buddha spoke the term "sat" (existence) in order to refute those of the future Sarvāstivāda school and others who cling to it as being the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although the single word "sat" also refers to existence, [the Buddha used the prefix *asat* to negate that].
However, the meaning of *satyārtha* (the meaning of truth) is now being explained;
therefore, the word *sat* expresses "falsity. The Sarvāstivādins say that *sat* has the meaning of "existence."
The *kāya* and so forth are as previously described;
although they are composite bodies, they are substantially existent.
"Body" (*kāya*) is a synonym for "self-entity" (*svabhāva*).
One should say that it is the view of self-substance (*svabhāva-dṛṣṭi*).
The Buddha spoke of "existence" (*sat*) in order to refute those such as the future Sautrāntikas who claim that this is a false view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although the term *sat* also refers to falsehood,
in this context one should say *asiddhi-sat* because it signifies the meaning of "existence.
Since *sat* expresses existence, in the Mahāyāna one should say *saṃgīti-sat*.
Thus, it is established as a transference.
For this reason, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is explained with both general and specific designations;
the term *sarvāstivāda* (or *sarvāstika*) refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The Sautrāntika school calls it the "false view of a self-body" (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
According to the intention of the present Mahāyāna,
it is the appearance resembling a self that manifests upon the mind.
Its essence is not substantially existent because it is a provisional phenomenon;
yet its essence is not entirely non-existent because the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) functions as an objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Since it is neither substantially existent nor merely illusory,
it is solely a phenomenon that arises through dependence and undergoes transformation.
That which is my basis of reliance:
furthermore, that which relies on the grasped object may be said to be false,
while that which relies on the transformed appearance may be said to exist.
Unlike other schools which hold [things] to be definitively real or definitively false,
it is called "transformation" (saṃkrānti);
this also includes that which belongs to the self (ātmīya).
It is not only the view of a self;
it may take the aggregates as its object either collectively or individually.
Discriminative [ignorance] and innate [ignorance] may take objects either collectively or individually,
as stated in the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
However, among these, the seventh consciousness takes only the mind as its object, conceiving it as the self.
Therefore, although it does not discern individual aggregates as distinct objects like that which arises through discrimination,
it nonetheless spontaneously takes them as distinct objects;
nevertheless, this view of self serves as its fundamental basis.
Because all views arise [from it],
it is called the basis for all modes of view (*sarvadṛṣṭigatāśraya*).
"Mode" (*gati*) means "analogy" (*upamā*).
Alternatively, it refers to the place of refuge.
The treatise states: "These distinctions of views are subsumed under those that arise from discrimination."
The commentary states:
Regarding the twenty phrases,
the *Abhidharma-prathama* says:
That is to say, for instance, reckoning that form is the self,
the self possesses form,
or form belongs to the self.
I am within form. One aggregate has four [aspects];
thus, the five aggregates comprise twenty phrases.
Among these twenty statements, five constitute the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*),
and fifteen constitute the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Why are there five views of self?
The fifteenth, "that which belongs to me," refers to that which is associated with what belongs to me and that which conforms to what belongs to me.
Because one does not depart from "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*).
There are fifteen kinds of what belongs to me,
as explained in detail through questions and answers in the first chapter of the *Abhidharma* (*Abhidharmapada*).
Because one discriminates the aggregates conditioned by conduct,
yet does not discriminate the place from which they arise,
there are twenty phrases.
The aggregates have "discriminative activity" as their condition.
"Activity" refers to the mode of activity,
namely the mode of activity characterized by "I" and "mine."
"Belonging to" means "mine.
Just as one discriminates the modes of "self" and "what belongs to self" only with respect to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
one does not discriminate the locus from which this aforementioned "what belongs to self" arises.
The notion of "mine" necessarily arises subsequent to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding what was said concerning the three types of non-conceptualization within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), this notion of "mine" takes which aggregate as its basis for conceiving it as a self? It arises from that [view of self].

[Question: One merely discriminates in general regarding "self" and "what belongs to self. When questioned, one does not discriminate or calculate that "the self is form," nor what this "what belongs to self" arises from.
Why, then, do you say only that one does not discriminate [the object]? [Answer: The "self" is the fundamental basis.
It does not arise from another.
Having already analyzed the statement that "form is the self," it is concluded.
It is not that their place of origin is not distinguished;

rather, because what belongs to "mine" necessarily arises subsequent to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), they are not the same. The sixty-two views and so forth should be understood accordingly. As for the sixty-five:
The first volume of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Miscellaneous Section, at the end of the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" chapter, section ten.
This analyzes [the dharmas] by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in this context:
"Such places" refers to the elements (*dhātu*). This means,
for example, taking form (*rūpa*) as the self (*ātman*).
Regarding each of the other four aggregates, there are three [perceptions]:
namely, "this is my ornament," "this is my servant," and so forth.
The "vessels of the self" consist of twelve types;
form constitutes one such self.
This totals thirteen. Thus,
within these five aggregates, there are sixty instances of "mine" and five views of self.
All these are the aggregates that serve as the conditions for discursive proliferation (*vikalpa*), and they are also the bases from which discursive proliferation arises.
Furthermore, these are what have arisen from discursive proliferation.
It is not something that arises simultaneously [with the aggregates], because the self that arises simultaneously is not conceptually imputed as distinct [from them].

What is meant by "delusion regarding the truth of suffering" and so forth?

that is, [the afflictions] that arise following views and doubt under each respective truth.

This would be a great error. Among these afflictions,
which ones are associated with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and which are not?

This question asks: what is the difference between agitation (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)?
[The] Treatise [says]:
"That makes it easy to understand; this makes it easy to take as an object.
[Commentary: Below, the Master of the Treatise provides the answer.
Restlessness (auddhatya) agitates the mind;
although the object is one, it causes the co-arising minds and mental factors to shift and change their interpretations repeatedly.
This is precisely the state where a single object is interpreted in multiple ways.
The function of distraction causes the mind to easily take other objects as its conditions;
that is, it allows a single moment of mind to easily engage with multiple objects.
Question: In the case of the five consciousnesses and so forth, or a single moment of defiled mind, how can one speak of "changing"?
Treatise:
Although it is but a single moment, there is the sense of transition toward existence.
Commentary states:
Although within a single moment of thought there is the understanding of two dharmas as objects,
even though there is no sense of simultaneous transformation,
because there is the sense of transformation and understanding through the continuity of many moments, [the object is established].
Although these two modes of activity exist within a single kṣaṇa, they are difficult to discern;
therefore, their modes of activity are revealed through their continuity.
If it were only a single thought-moment, they would remain hidden and thus are not described.

If that were so, then in all defiled states of mind, the power of restlessness (*auddhatya*) should always be easily discernible, and the power of distraction (*vikṣepa*) should likewise always be easily discernible; why is this not the case?
If one discerns a single object with a single mind, the object of cognition is not easily changed.
All defiled minds should likewise lack these two [characteristics],
such as the meditative absorption of relishing (*āsvādana-samādhi*),
wherein both the object of focus and the mode of engagement remain unchanged.
Because these two do not exist, the treatise states:
"At the time of an afflicted mind, [the afflictions] reach and pervade the afflicted mind."
The commentary states:
In response to this question,
it is said that when the mind is defiled, by virtue of these two powers, it should constantly and moment by moment be easily liberated and easily redirected toward its objects.
Because the power of innate mindfulness, meditative concentration, and so forth has increased,
one restrains and maintains these two [body and mind] like tethering a monkey;
thus, the innate defiled mind abides for a time, focusing single-mindedly on a single object.
The power of restlessness (*auddhatya*) is slight, yet its substance is not non-existent; this is as when restlessness increases,
because factors such as mindfulness (*smṛti*) and concentration (*samādhi*) have inferior modes of activity (*ākāra*),
resulting in their mutual increase or diminution.
Therefore, as explained in various treatises, these two factors both pervade all defiled minds.
The treatise asks:
Why is it that lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) leads to many transgressions?
The commentary states:
It is not that one is dull-witted due to delusion regarding objects;
rather, erroneous and false understanding is what is termed "incorrect awareness" (asamprajanya).
One who lacks correct awareness generates much karma;
one frequently initiates unwholesome physical and verbal actions,
and frequently transgresses the precepts and so forth.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-saṃgraha-śāstra* are identical in their treatment of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Both treatises are the same.
There is an interpretation that non-apprehension (asaṃprajanya) extends up to its association with wisdom (*prajñā*).
The commentary states:
"The first master."
Because the Abhidharma states that these are wisdoms associated with the various afflictions. According to one interpretation in the treatise,
non-apprehension (*asamprajanya*) is designated as "non-apprehension" once it reaches that state.
The commentary states:
This second master is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*).
Fifty-five [factors] are called "parts of delusion" (*moha-bhāga*).
Thus, for those who possess both [wisdom and delusion], that which causes one to know what is incorrect is termed "incorrect knowledge" (*ayoniśo-jñāna*).
This concludes the mutual reconciliation of the texts by the two aforementioned masters.
All of these are *niṣyanda* (outflow) results, established according to what is grasped as definitive;
however, because they are easy to understand,
I shall not elaborate on each one individually.
All [points] should be understood according to the preceding discussion. The *Śāstra* states:
There is an interpretation that incorrect awareness (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) extends throughout all defiled minds.
The commentary states:
This third master takes the two as the essence.
The second [point] is because of the scriptural authority cited previously.
Regarding the fifty-fifth [topic], it is stated that [the afflictions] pervade all defiled minds;
as for those statements that they do not so pervade, these are due to a specific underlying meaning.
As previously stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*,
the words "and" (*ca*) and "as well as" (*api*) extend [the application] up to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The commentary states:
From here below is the fourth section, explaining the preceding verse’s mention of deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*),
arrogance (*mada*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), and so forth.
The words "and," "furthermore," and "also" indicate that there are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) in addition to the twenty.
As explained in the *Dharmaskandha* regarding the *Saṃyuktāgama*,
there are many secondary afflictions.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its eighty-eighth and fifty-eighth fascicles, also cites this sutra;
yet those of the old school were unaware of this and claimed it belonged to the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
Some say that the *Vinaya* explains this in the *Kṣudravastuka*,
arguing that although they are called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), they are not included within the category of primary afflictions (*kleśa*).
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the fifth section, explaining the names of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and their scope of application.
The eighty-eight instances of greed and so forth are also termed secondary afflictions.
The seventh chapter of the Abhidharma also contains this meaning:
all afflictions are "concomitants," yet there are concomitants that are not afflictions.
As explained extensively in the *Dharmaskandha-pāda* and other treatises—
namely, regarding anger and so forth, as well as the sixty-two views—
the states such as "proceeding forward" and so on are of the same category as the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Defiled phenomena are merely termed "concomitants" because they are outflows of the afflictions;
they are not termed "afflictions" themselves because they are not the root.
Since there are many types that are all termed "concomitants" (anuvartin),
why is it that only twenty are mentioned here? [The Treatise says:]
"Only twenty [factors] are taught because they are exclusively defiled and coarse.
The commentary states:
From here below is the sixth section, which explains their establishment and rejection.
This refers to three meanings.
Although greed and the other [afflictions] are concomitants, they are not mentioned here because these twenty are not themselves afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, greed and the others are excluded.
Although unwholesome desires and other such factors are also concomitants,
their essential natures as distinct-object mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*) pervade all three moral natures;
since these [mental factors under discussion] are exclusively defiled, those others are not mentioned here.
However, because forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and the like are subdivisions of delusion (*moha*), they are mentioned as such;
they are not mentioned as subdivisions of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Since forgetfulness is subsumed within the category of delusion, there is no fault of over-extension (*aniyata-doṣa*) in this regard.
Although "proceeding forward" and so forth are also modes of activity (*anuvartana*),
because their characteristics are subtle,
these [characteristics] are merely coarse.
Therefore, it possesses these three characteristics:
first, it is not an affliction;
second, it is exclusively defiled.
Because three [of the remaining factors] are coarse, only twenty are mentioned and no others are spoken of.
Treatise.
The remaining defiled dharmas should be understood accordingly as appropriate.
The commentary states:
"However, regarding these twenty [dharmas], there are other defiled dharmas external to them."
For example, wrong desire and so forth are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of these [roots].
"Outflow" means being of the same kind (*sabhāga*).
Alternatively, this state does not exist apart from its substance;
it exists upon these actual dharmas, such as lack of faith and so forth.
The remaining conventional phenomena are also established as designations.

Furthermore, these various conventional phenomena are designated by names upon the basis of substantial entities such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth; they are merely designations for these particular states (*avasthā*).
Due to differences in their states,
or because they are their outflows—
namely, bodily and vocal actions— they are also called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These are its outflows;
because they are originated by various secondary afflictions (upakleśa),
they are all subsumed within these twenty mentioned here.
One should understand this according to their respective categories as appropriate.

Having examined each of these eighty-eight [factors], one sees that they are precisely what is not mentioned here in the *Mahāśāstra* regarding phenomena such as wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and so forth. This is the reason for their omission.
Treatise:
These twenty [points] should be understood as previously explained. Commentary:
From here below is the second section: the analysis by way of various categories.
Within this analysis by way of various categories, there is a further analysis by means of thirteen distinct categories.
First is the distinction between the nominal and the real.
Among these ten minor afflictions, such as anger and so forth, forgetfulness, heedlessness, and lack of clear comprehension are not distinct from the [major] disputes.
The *Abhidharma-prathama* states: "It should be known that anger and the others are all nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*)."
Although this is stated in general terms that among the individual [categories] there are both real and nominal [entities],
furthermore, whatever exists by way of other-characteristics (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) is collectively termed "nominal existence.
Such are these thirteen [categories].
It is called "provisional" (prajñapti) because it exists only in part;
for example, the other seven factors— lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), lack of faith (āśraddhya), and laziness (kausīdya)— are necessarily substantially existent (dravyasat),
yet they are also termed provisional when described according to their dependence on other characteristics.
The first thirteen are provisional,
while the latter four are real;
this is established by both scripture and reasoning.

Fifty-fifth: because the four factors such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth are said to exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*), even those that are merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are also conventionally existent.
It is only in relation to the ultimate (*paramārtha*) that they are termed "conventional."
Yet their essence exists substantially;
these statements refer to the conventional in relation to the ultimate.
Because they follow after the characteristics of others, their essence is not provisional;
however, there is an interpretation that the three— restlessness, torpor, and agitation— are provisional.
There is an interpretation that this is real, because it is as previously stated; therefore, taking the real as superior is now adopted.
Although each was explained individually above, [the real is taken here].
Since it has not yet been shown in total how many among the twenty are provisional and how many are real,
we shall now distinguish them collectively.
Treatise:
All twenty are common to both because they arise through the power of [their respective] forces.
The commentary states:
This is the second section, the gate of co-arising and conceptualization.
This is based on the correct interpretation.
In the section below concerning the "gate of abandonment," some say that it consists of cultivation alone;
however, we do not rely on that view here.
Because they are not correct,
each one pertains to both [types of affliction],
as they arise in accordance with the two types of delusion.
Because those ten factors, such as anger (*krodha*), are also metaphorically established upon greed (*rāga*) and the others following the [four] views (*dṛṣṭi*),
this shall be understood in detail below.
Treatise:
Among these twenty [mental factors], each takes its turn as the primary factor. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Third, the section on mutual correspondence:
among the ten minor [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, they definitely do not arise simultaneously with one another,
because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are mutually contradictory.
Why is this so? Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse and violent,
unlike the fundamental [meditation], which is subtle and harmonious.
Because each functions as a primary [mental factor] individually, they do not arise simultaneously.
This is stated in both [sections] fifty-five and fifty-eight, which say that the ten factors such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth do not coexist with one another.
It is exactly the same as this. According to the treatise,
among the two types of "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*), both are capable of arising simultaneously.
The commentary states:
Among the factors such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*),
two are associated with all unwholesome minds.
However, because they exist in all unwholesome minds,
the sixth, fifty-fifth, and fifty-eighth [sections] of the Abhidharma-kośa are identical in this regard, as previously explained.
Thus, one should know that acquisition (*prāpti*) arises simultaneously with both the small and the great [categories of defilements],
as it is common to all unwholesome states (*akuśala*).
This point is supported by the meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58.
It is taught that the eight major factors, such as restlessness (auddhatya) and so forth, pervade all defiled minds;
they relate to one another reciprocally,
as well as with the twelve minor and middling factors.
All [of these] can coexist,
as they do not contradict one another.
As stated in the fourth fascicle [of this treatise], there were four masters.
The fourth master’s position is correct,
because forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension are subdivisions of delusion (*moha*),
whereas distraction has a distinct nature of its own.
The remainder is established by common consensus;
therefore, these eight are universal.
Within this context, there is only the correct position of the latter master.
Treatise:
There are passages stating that the six [consciousnesses] do not arise simultaneously.
Commentary: This means...
If all eight [factors] are universally defiled,
why does the *Pañcāśatikā* state that five or five are not universally defiled?
Because it excludes torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Because these two modes of activity do not arise simultaneously when they increase, one must necessarily be predominant while the other is subordinate, just as in the Sarvāstivāda system regarding the two dharmas of *vitarka* and *vicāra*. Question: What are the coarse and subtle characteristics of *vitarka* and *vicāra*?
It is not permitted for [the two] to exist simultaneously in a single mind.
Lethargy and restlessness have the characteristics of sinking and elevation;
they should not coexist in a single mind. Answer: They are distinct entities; as one sinks and the other elevates, they increase alternately.
Laxity and torpor, as well as restlessness and agitation, arise together;
however, because they lack substantial reality and their coarse and subtle aspects do not mutually correspond,
they do not coexist within a single moment of mind.
The modes of activity of both [vitarka and vicāra] increase, yet they are mutually opposed by the characteristics of lethargy (styāna) and restlessness (auddhatya).

At times when they increase or do not increase, their essential nature does not conflict. Question: Regarding the characteristics of vitarka and vicāra as coarse and subtle—by what criteria are they determined as coarse and subtle?
Question: Are the characteristics of lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) high or low?
Do they increase or not increase? Answer: They do not have separate substantial entities (*dravya*), being merely designated (*prajñapti*) as such;
therefore, it is so. These [two] do have separate substantial entities and are real; therefore, they are able to be thus. Question: Should this also apply to greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*)?
"Is there also increase and non-increase? Answer:
"No, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fixed, and the essence of restlessness and so forth is pervasive."
The modes of activity (ākāra) vary in intensity;
they are not like vitarka and vicāra, whose essence is non-pervasive,
and thus cannot be used as an analogy.
It is simply that when the modes of activity of lethargy (*styāna*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) increase together, they do not arise simultaneously;
it is not that their two substances do not arise together. [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya]
In some places, it is stated that [the factors] exist only up to the point of opposition because they are exclusively wholesome.
The commentary states:
Among the six categories of the Abhidharma, five are said to be universal.
These are the five factors: lack of faith, laziness, lethargy, restlessness, and heedlessness.
These five factors oppose exclusively wholesome states;
lethargy and restlessness obstruct pliancy.
The obstruction to equanimity (*upekṣā*) is now set forth; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
This is not like forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and so forth, which are admitted to contradict the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Although mindfulness (*smṛti*) and the others possess a portion of delusion (*moha*), they nevertheless contradict non-delusion (*amoha*).
It is not mentioned because it does not constitute a factor of delusion;
furthermore, although the mindfulness that opposes it is wholesome,
mindfulness itself pervades all three moral natures.
This is not analogous to the case within wholesome dharmas, and thus does not serve as a precedent for the argument.
The treatise states: because this [ignorance] is exclusively defiled, it may exist up to the five sensory consciousnesses.
The commentary states:
The fourth section concerns the gate of the simultaneous occurrence of various consciousnesses;
it should be understood that there are eight, seven, or six consciousnesses.
The eight are as explained in the third fascicle;
the seven are as explained in the fifth fascicle.
These include the factors of delusion, mindfulness, and so forth.
The factors of equanimity and mindfulness, such as mindfulness itself, are subtle;
whereas the ten minor afflictions, such as anger and so forth, have coarse and violent aspects.
Since the five consciousnesses are subtle in comparison to those [afflictions], they do not coexist with them.
The two intermediate [realms] have eight;
the five consciousnesses may exist in the great [desire realm].
Because they are entirely unwholesome and defiled. According to the treatise,
for this reason, the intermediate [level] is associated with five feelings.
The commentary states:
The fifth is the section on association with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*).
Among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), there are four remaining [to be discussed].
The meaning is certainly not stated [explicitly] because it pervades the unwholesome and so forth;
it is said that the medium and great [degrees] pervade all five feelings.
The five feelings are all associated with the unwholesome because they are defiled;
this is the meaning of the treatise. According to one interpretation, among the ten minor [unwholesome mental factors], four are associated with [the feelings] excluding suffering.
The commentary states:
This first master excludes the seven [mental factors] other than flattery, deceit, and pride— namely, anger and the rest.
Only the three feelings of pleasure, sorrow, and equanimity arise together;
they do not extend to the higher realms because of the absence of mental volition (*āśaya*).
It does not exist within the five consciousnesses.
In the desire realm, it is not associated with suffering or pleasure,
because in the hells, the mental consciousness does not experience suffering.
The universal factors associated with joy and grief also possess joy;
thus, flattery (*māyā*), deception (*śāṭhya*), and arrogance (*mada*) are associated with four feelings, excluding suffering,
because they coexist with pleasure in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because there is the mental disposition (*āśaya*) of the first dhyāna.
According to one interpretation, [the afflictions] such as anger have already been discussed previously.
The commentary states:
Regarding this second master,
[he asserts that] seven [of these factors] are exclusively bound to the desire realm.
In the four [mental factors] associated with feeling, pleasure is excluded,
because there is no pleasure in the mental consciousness of the desire realm.
Flattery, deception, and conceit arise together with five types of feeling.
This refers to the increase of suffering,
because there is the experience of painful sensation within the mind,
as has been explained previously.
Regarding these aspects associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta-ākāra*):
the treatise states that these characteristics concomitant with feeling are as explained in the section on the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The commentary states:
Question: How can anger and the like coexist with joy?
How can stinginess and the like accompany sorrow?
This is as explained previously in the section on the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). The treatise states:
"The true meaning is thus, up to and including the meaning of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-artha*)."
The commentary states:
What has been explained above is according to the meaning of subtle analysis.
As for that which follows the coarse characteristics:
First, because they arise for the most part in accordance with a single aspect;
second, because they follow the characteristics of the Hīnayāna:
the five factors, beginning with anger (*krodha*), are associated only with mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because it is a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*),
and because it functions as a state of dejection (*daurmanasya*), concealment (*mrakṣa*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*) are associated with joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Those [factors] belonging to the categories of greed and delusion involve this mode of joyful activity; furthermore,
the other three— flattery, deceit, and pride— increase the experience of pleasant feeling.
Because the higher stages exist,
the two [faculties] of suffering and sorrow are excluded; for there,
only the mode of joyful activity prevails.
The medium and great [degrees] are coarser than the subtle;
this is also as previously explained according to their actual meaning,
because they function through both adverse and favorable modes of activity.
Treatise:
Thus, up to twenty [categories], because they are not mutually contradictory. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Sixth is the gate of association with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
All of them can arise together,
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not contradict one another.
This concludes the general explanation.
Below follows a question and answer addressing specific difficulties.
Question: How can forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā) coexist with mindfulness (smṛti)?
How can corrupt wisdom coexist with wisdom?
The treatise states:
because defiled mindfulness and defiled wisdom can also attain association (*saṃprayoga*).
The commentary states:
Herein, that which takes forgetfulness as its essence does not coexist with the mindfulness belonging to the category of specific objects.
As for those that pervade the category of delusion (*moha*), they are therefore associated with it;
wisdom (*prajñā*) should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, because there is also a portion of delusion,
these two are combined and thus described as "defiled mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth."
Question: Anger takes the present as its object, while mindfulness takes what was previously practiced as its object.
How can these two be said to arise simultaneously?
Treatise:
Mindfulness also takes the present as its object and can likewise attain association.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Mindfulness takes that which was previously practiced as its object; it also takes present objects as its object.
Among these, there are categories that were previously practiced in the past.
Therefore, since mindfulness also arises with the present as its object, it can coexist with anger.
For example, when one sees an old enemy and gives rise to anger, one then recollects the Dharma;
this is a case where mindfulness follows the movement of anger.
Below, anger follows the movement of thought;
since thought takes the immediately preceding past moment as its object,
it is also said to take the past as its object.
Because of the present single moment of thought,
the state of the object of anger is present;
when the matter is brought to completion according to the circumstances, it is called "present as an object."
Furthermore, anger also takes the past moment as its object;
thus, the two dharmas of anger and mindfulness are both compatible with their respective modes of activity,
and there is no fault.
Question: Concentration (samādhi) focuses on a single object, whereas distraction (vikṣepa) apprehends multiple conditions.
How can these two arise simultaneously?
Treatise:
When a defiled meditative absorption arises, there is no fault in its reaching the associated [factors].
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Since that which arises when defiled concentration occurs is itself termed "defiled," and since the mind is likewise agitated, there is no contradiction; thus,
there is no fault in their association.
It is not that distraction necessarily takes many objects;
for agitation is the intrinsic characteristic of distraction.
Treatise.
"Two in the middle, eight in the great, and eighty associated with the afflictions.
The commentary states:
This is the seventh gate, the gate of association with the fundamental [afflictions].
Section Two: The eight great [afflictions] are associated with all defiled minds and with all unwholesome states.
However, that which is innate co-exists with other innate factors; among these innate factors,
it excludes the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi),
and it does not co-exist with shamelessness (āhrīkya) or lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
Because their intrinsic natures are contradictory,
others are necessarily able to coexist.
Treatise.
The ten small [meditations] certainly do not reach that [state], because they lack subtlety and precision.
The commentary states:
"The nature and substance of the ten small practices are both coarse and agitated."
Because the aspects (*ākāra*) of those views and doubt are subtle,
what was previously stated regarding anger, doubt, and one portion of the two views being associated with them was said in reference to their subtle aspects.
Now, anger and the like involve coarse modes of activity that are mutually contradictory;
thus, they do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, hatred and envy cease because of indecision caused by doubt regarding the [Truths of] Cessation and the Path.
Thus, there is no fault even if [the mind] is accompanied by aversion and so forth;
this is stated in terms of the majority of cases,
and it is not contradictory.
Treatise:
Because the five factors, such as anger (*krodha*), are branches of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Commentary states:
Anger, resentment, vexation, envy, and harmfulness can coexist with both conceit and delusion,
but they cannot coexist with both greed and hatred.
Because it is diametrically opposed to the meditative concentration associated with greed,
and because hatred is the essential nature of anger and the like;
by this, it is proven.
The states of forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension associated with the unique ignorance do not pervade this mind,
because they are themselves portions of delusion.
This point should be considered:
it is not stated that non-concomitant ignorance necessarily arises together [with the afflictions],
but rather that it arises together with the ten [afflictions].
At this very time of ignorance,
although there may be a factor of wisdom,
the factor of delusion necessarily pervades all collections of defiled minds.
It is not that the single dharma of non-associated ignorance is necessarily accompanied by unwholesome discernment; rather,
it is within this aggregate of ignorance [that such occurs].
Because other dharmas coexist with this,
[ignorance] is provisionally established based upon them.
Treatise.
Because stinginess, delusion, and pride all reach the state of being part of greed.
The commentary states:
Stinginess, delusion, and pride—these two [latter] dharmas may coexist.
Because it is not associated with greed due to its intrinsic nature;
because it is not associated with hatred due to its opposition to it.
Treatise.
"Haughtiness (mada) is associated only with delusion (moha), because it is a derivative of craving.
The commentary states:
"Haughtiness is associated only with delusion."
Because it is a derivative of greed (*lobha*),
it does not coexist with hatred (*dveṣa*) or greed;
it differs from pride (*māna*).
It does not coexist with conceit (*māna*).
Arrogance (*mada*) arises from exalting oneself by taking one's own qualities as its object; conceit also arises from looking down upon others.
Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. According to the treatise,
concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*) belong to the category of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).
The commentary states:
These three coexist with greed, delusion, and pride;
because their modes of activity (ākāra) are not contradictory, they coexist with them.
Because it is a derivative of greed and delusion, it does not coexist with hatred;
because it is a derivative of greed, it is conjoined with delusion;
and because it is a derivative of delusion, it coexists with greed.
However, this should be considered:
while the concealment (*mrakṣa*) and other factors that are subdivisions of greed may coexist with anger,
how could the concealment and other factors that are subdivisions of independent delusion (*moha*) do so?
